extracted.intended_audience: crisis managers, public relations professionals, communications students and researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria from Situational Crisis Communication Theory (Coombs) for assessing crises and selecting strategic communication responses to protect organizational reputation. Useful for crisis managers, PR officers drafting statements/press releases, and researchers studying crisis response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match strategic response to crisis responsibility and reputational threat
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT suggests that crisis managers should match strategic crisis responses to the level of crisis responsibility and reputational threat posed by a crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core principle: choose post-crisis actions based on the crisis situation. Understanding how stakeholders will attribute responsibility and perceive reputational threat should guide which communication strategies (deny, diminish, rebuild, bolstering, informing) are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate crisis using three elements: crisis type, crisis history, prior relationship reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating the crisis type, crisis history and prior relationship reputation will help crisis managers predict the level of reputational threat and stakeholder attributions of responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three elements form the basis for predicting reputational harm and selecting a response strategy. They should be assessed together — e.g., a low-responsibility crisis with a bad crisis history may still pose elevated threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial crisis responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial crisis responsibility is how much the organization's stakeholders attribute the crisis to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine stakeholder attributions early: high attribution implies greater reputational threat and typically requires stronger remedial responses (e.g., rebuild). Low attribution may allow informational or diminish responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis history
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the organization has faced similar crises in the past; a history of similar crises increases attributions of responsibility and reputational threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If crisis history exists, it intensifies stakeholder attributions and usually moves the recommended response toward more corrective/rebuilding actions even if initial responsibility appears low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior relational reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: How well the organization has treated its stakeholders in the past; prior relationship reputation influences attributions and reputational threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A neutral or positive prior reputation can buffer reputational harm; a negative prior reputation amplifies threat. Consider past stakeholder interactions when deciding tone and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify crisis into clusters and subtypes (victim, accidental, intentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coombs identifies three crisis clusters: victim cluster (organization also a victim), accidental cluster (organizational actions unintentional), and intentional/preventable cluster (organization knowingly at fault). Each cluster contains specific crisis types (e.g., natural disaster, rumor, workplace violence; technical-error accidents; human-error product harm; organizational misdeeds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifying the crisis into the correct cluster and subtype is the first step for predicting stakeholder attributions and selecting an appropriate response strategy. Use the provided subtypes list to map the event (e.g., rumor → victim cluster; technical-error product harm → accidental cluster; management misconduct → intentional cluster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing and adjusting information as a sufficient response (Table 1, item 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informing and adjusting information alone can be enough when crises have minimal attributions of crisis responsibility (victim crises), no history of similar crises and a neutral or positive prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factual, corrective information and updates when the organization is clearly a victim and has a clean history; avoid over-apologizing or overcommitting resources unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use victimage as part of the response for certain crisis types (Table 1, item 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Victimage can be used as part of the response for workplace violence, product tampering, natural disasters and rumors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remind stakeholders that the organization is also a victim when appropriate to reduce attributions of responsibility; ensure claims of victimhood are credible and evidence-based to avoid backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diminish strategies for victim crises with history/negative reputation (Table 1, item 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish crisis response strategies should be used for crises with minimal attributions of crisis responsibility (victim crises) coupled with a history of similar crises and/or negative prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reputation or history increases perceived responsibility, combine diminishing tactics (excuse, justification) with credible evidence to reduce perceived severity or responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diminish strategies for accidental crises with no history and neutral/positive reputation (Table 1, item 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish crisis response strategies should be used for crises with low attributions of crisis responsibility (accident crises), which have no history of similar crises, and a neutral or positive prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accidental crises that lack a damaging history may be managed by minimizing perceived responsibility and showing cause was unintentional; provide evidence to support the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rebuild strategies for accidental crises with history or negative prior reputation (Table 1, item 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild crisis response strategies should be used for crises with low attributions of crisis responsibility (accident crises), coupled with a history of similar crises and/or negative prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When history or reputation worsens stakeholder perceptions even for accidents, adopt rebuild tactics (compensation, apology) to repair trust and reduce long-term reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rebuild strategies for preventable crises regardless of history or prior reputation (Table 1, item 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild crisis response strategies should be used for crises with strong attributions of crisis responsibility (preventable crises) regardless of crisis history or prior relationship reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the organization is clearly at fault (intentional/preventable), prioritize rebuilding: accept responsibility, apologize, offer compensation and corrective action plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use deny posture for rumors and challenges when possible (Table 1, item 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deny posture crisis response strategies should be used for rumor and challenge crises, when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If credible evidence shows no organizational involvement, use denial/scapegoating/attack-the-accuser tactics carefully to sever perceived connections. Ensure evidence supports denial; unsupported denials can backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistency in crisis response strategies; avoid mixing deny with diminish/rebuild (Table 1, item 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistency in crisis response strategies. Mixing deny crisis response strategies with either the diminish or rebuild strategies will erode the effectiveness of the overall response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a coherent response posture. Switching between conflicting strategies confuses stakeholders and reduces message credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary crisis response strategies (deny, diminish, rebuild) and their purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Coombs identified three primary response groups: deny (sever perceived connection), diminish (assure publics crisis not as bad or org had little to do with it), and rebuild (offer aid/ask forgiveness to change perceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select primary strategy based on attributions and reputational threat. Deny aims to eliminate perceived responsibility, diminish to reduce perceived severity/responsibility (requires credible evidence), rebuild to provide compensation/apology and restore reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deny strategy tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Deny crisis response strategies include: Attack the accuser (confront claimant), Denial (assert there is no crisis), Scapegoat (blame external person/group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the organization is demonstrably not responsible or when a rumor/challenge can be credibly refuted. Consider legal and relational consequences of attacking accusers or scapegoating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminish strategy tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish crisis response strategies include: Excuse (minimize responsibility by denying intent or control) and Justification (minimize perceived damage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diminish requires credible evidence and careful framing to avoid appearing evasive. Use when responsibility is low or can be plausibly downplayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild strategy tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild crisis response strategies include: Compensation (offer money or gifts to victims) and Apology (take full responsibility and ask forgiveness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuild is appropriate when responsibility is strong or history/reputation amplifies threat. Combine apologies with concrete corrective actions to restore trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary strategy: Bolstering and its tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Bolstering attempts to increase positive perceptions by presenting new positive information or reminding stakeholders of past good works (Reminder, Ingratiation, Victimage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolstering should supplement primary strategies, not replace them. Used to arouse sympathy or reinforce goodwill, but avoid using bolstering to deflect from necessary apologies or corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of crisis response strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis response strategies have three objectives relative to protecting reputations: (1) shape attributions of the crisis, (2) change perceptions of the organization in crisis, and (3) reduce the negative effect generated by the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting tactics, evaluate how each will influence attributions, perceptions, and negative outcomes. Measure success by shifts in stakeholder attributions, sentiment, and behavior where possible.
